issues.description: State machine collapse from 4 to 3 states changes the meaning of `walking` and the cycle-detection contract
issues.detail: Pre-change, `working` meant 'descendants being explored' and `walking` was distinct. After the change, `walking` is now reused for the 'descendants being explored' state. The `push` function still consults the state: when a node is encountered whose state is `walking`, push() calls `slicesx.LastIndexFunc` to locate it on the stack — this is a cycle-detection path that previously only fired for `working`. State the invariant explicitly in a comment: 'walking == node is on the stack with children being expanded; sorted == node has been emitted; unsorted == never seen'. Without that comment a reader cannot reconstruct why push() does an O(n) scan of the stack in this branch.

issues.description: Cycle-detection branch in push() is O(stack) per repeated visit — asymptotic claim deserves audit
issues.detail: When `push` is called on a node already in the `walking` state, it performs `slicesx.LastIndexFunc` over the entire stack. In a pathological DAG with wide fan-in to a shared ancestor, this turns the overall sort from O(V+E) into something closer to O(E * V). The PR does not change this behavior, but the state rename invites scrutiny: state the worst-case complexity in a comment, or replace the linear scan with a map lookup of stack position. ASYMPTOTICALLY-OK-PRACTICALLY-SLOW for dense graphs.

issues.description: Termination/emit invariant changed subtly: `s.state[k] = sorted` now only set when yield() succeeds normally
issues.detail: Previously, `s.state[k] = sorted` was set unconditionally after the pop, even when yield returned false (causing an early `return`). Now it is set only inside the `if !yield(node)` success branch. Because the deferred `clear(s.state)` runs on every Sort exit, this is observationally fine for the current call — state is wiped regardless. But the invariant 'a node popped from the stack has state == sorted' no longer holds during the brief window between pop and the deferred clear. State this in a comment, or hoist the assignment back outside the yield branch to preserve the simpler invariant. Currently UNDER-AUDITED.

issues.description: Defer-based cleanup hides a non-trivial reset; document why both `clear(s.stack)` and `s.stack = s.stack[:0]` are needed
issues.detail: `clear(s.stack)` zeroes the underlying array (so retained Node references can be GC'd), then `s.stack = s.stack[:0]` resets length while preserving capacity. This is the correct idiom for a pooled slice that holds pointers, but a reader who hasn't internalized Go 1.21+ `clear` semantics on slices will wonder why both lines are present. A one-line literate comment — 'clear zeroes entries so Nodes can be collected; the reslice keeps capacity for reuse' — would prevent a future maintainer from 'simplifying' this to one line.

issues.description: Comment update introduces two spelling errors and reduces clarity rather than improving it
issues.detail: The replacement comment reads 'whether this node has been visisted and if its the first or second visit'. 'visisted' should be 'visited'; 'its' should be 'it's'. More importantly, the prior comment named the mechanism ('the visited stack tracks...') while the new comment is vaguer ('the state tracks...'). For a literate-programming-grade comment on the load-bearing DFS loop, name the three state values and the transition diagram inline: unsorted -> walking (first visit, push children) -> sorted (second visit, emit).

issues.description: Removed `s.stack = s.stack[0:]` had a different intent than the new `s.stack = s.stack[:0]` in defer
issues.detail: The removed line `s.stack = s.stack[0:]` was a no-op reslice (length unchanged) — the PR title 'fixes non-zero elements in the stack slice' suggests the author believed this line was zeroing the stack, which it wasn't. The new defer correctly does `clear` + `[:0]`. Worth noting in the commit message that the prior line was an outright bug, not just suboptimal — the reset to empty was never happening at entry. Now the invariant 'stack is empty on entry to Sort()' depends on the prior call's defer running. Document that.

issues.description: No test added to demonstrate the bug being fixed
issues.detail: The PR title says 'Fix state reuse for internal/toposort' but the diff contains no test exercising back-to-back Sort() calls on a reused Sorter. 'Beware of bugs in the above code; I have only proved it correct, not tried it.' A test that calls Sort() twice on the same Sorter and asserts identical output would pin this behavior and prevent regression. Without it, the fix is UNDER-AUDITED in the sense that future refactors won't be caught.

review.summary: The diff correctly addresses real state-reuse bugs: the prior `s.stack = s.stack[0:]` was a no-op (not a zeroing as the title implies), and resetting state at end-of-iteration via defer is cleaner than at-entry. Collapsing the four-state machine to three is plausible but the new meaning of `walking` (covering what used to be `working`) is not documented, and push()'s O(stack) cycle-detection scan now hangs off that renamed state — the asymptotic claim for the whole sort deserves a stated invariant. The replacement comment introduces two spelling errors ('visisted', 'its') and is vaguer than what it replaces; a literate-programming-grade comment naming the three states and their transitions belongs on the DFS loop. The cleanup idiom `clear(s.stack); s.stack = s.stack[:0]` is correct Go-1.21+ practice but worth a one-line comment so a future maintainer doesn't 'simplify' it. UNDER-AUDITED overall — fix is right but the analysis and a regression test are missing.
